sections.heading: Asking to be led by Jesus
sections.text: Lord Jesus, please give me the mercy of being led by you. Teach me to pay attention to your Word and to the wise boundaries of your providence. When you give me hard things, do not let them deaden my heart. Use even the bitter parts of life to wake me up, sharpen my faith, and make me more alive to you.
theological_themes: Christ personally leads his people through Scripture and providence.
Hard providences can be used by God for growth rather than spiritual collapse.
The believer asks for grace to receive suffering as under Christ's wise care.

scripture_references.connection: This passage presents God's Word as the light by which his people walk, which supports the prayer's request to be directed by Scripture rather than by confusion or impulse.
James teaches that trials can produce endurance and maturity in believers, grounding the request that bitter things would enliven and strengthen faith rather than crush it.

sections.heading: Needing help when I am discouraged and tempted
sections.text: When I am low and unsure, give me enough encouragement to keep following you. As you once dealt patiently with Gideon, remove what is needlessly discouraging me and give me courage for the next obedient step. And when temptation presses in, let me hide under the shelter of your compassion, knowing you understand weakness and know how to help me.
theological_themes: God can strengthen weak faith with patient encouragement.
Christ sympathizes with tempted believers and gives timely help.
The believer depends on Christ rather than self-confidence in temptation.

scripture_references.connection: Gideon's request for signs is not presented as a model for demanding proof from God, but it does show God's patient kindness toward a fearful servant whom he is strengthening for obedience.
Hebrews grounds confidence in prayer in the sympathy of Jesus, who was tempted yet without sin, making it directly relevant to seeking help under temptation.

sections.heading: Thanking you that you have not let me go
sections.text: Thank you that I am still in your hand. You have not thrown me away like a star gone dark or left me drifting like a boat with no rudder. Keep my life in your service. Do not let me live merely to take up space, but make my remaining days useful in the work you give me.
theological_themes: Christ preserves his people and does not abandon them.
A believer's life is meant for God-given usefulness, not self-directed existence.
Gratitude grows from knowing one is held by Christ.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus says his sheep are known, kept, and held securely in his hand, which directly supports the prayer's gratitude for not being cast off or abandoned.
Paul teaches that believers are created in Christ for good works prepared by God, grounding the desire that one's life remain useful in God's purposes.

sections.heading: Keeping me from being crushed or provoked into sin
sections.text: Do not let me be trampled by pride, injustice, money, status, or the selfish power of other people. And when I am treated wrongly, keep me from anger that runs ahead of you. Help me wait for you patiently and quietly. Guard my mouth so I do not speak foolishly in the heat of the moment.
theological_themes: God's people ask for protection from oppressive worldly powers and corrupt desires.
Waiting on God is an act of trust, especially under injustice.
Sinful anger and reckless speech must be resisted by grace.

scripture_references.connection: This psalm calls God's people to wait for the Lord and not give way to anger over evildoers, which fits the prayer's plea for patience instead of rash outrage.
James warns that human anger does not produce God's righteousness, supporting the request for restraint in speech and temper.

sections.heading: Giving you my heart and my will
sections.text: Let your mercy stay with me for as long as I live. Help me hand myself over to your will, not grudgingly, but because I trust you. Take my heart and keep it in your hand. Write reverence for you so deeply into me that neither time nor eternity can erase it.
theological_themes: God's covenant mercy accompanies his people through life.
Surrender to God's will rests on trust in his goodness.
True reverence is something God writes into the heart, not something the believer can manufacture.

scripture_references.connection: David's confidence that God's goodness and mercy will follow him throughout life gives biblical shape to the prayer's request for mercy to accompany the believer while living.
God promises to give his people a new heart and put his Spirit within them, supporting the prayer's plea that God would take the heart and make it reverent and responsive to him.

sections.heading: Committing myself to your covenant grace
sections.text: I entrust myself to your grace and to the care of your covenant—in sickness and in health, in whatever comes. I do this because you have overcome the world, fulfilled God's law, completed the righteousness that justifies sinners, swallowed up death in victory, and received all authority in heaven and on earth. Let this covenant be marked with your own blood in the court of forgiving mercy. Put your name on it—the name I trust—because the only signature I can bring is the weak and unworthy hand of a mortal sinner who belongs to you.
theological_themes: The believer's confidence rests on Christ's finished saving work, not personal worthiness.
Christ's blood secures the new covenant and forgiveness of sins.
Jesus has conquered the world, defeated death, and received universal authority.
Personal commitment to God is real, but it is upheld by Christ's covenant grace.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus identifies the cup with the new covenant in his blood, directly grounding the prayer's confidence that covenant mercy is sealed by Christ's blood.
Jesus tells his disciples to take heart because he has overcome the world, which supports the prayer's confidence in him amid whatever circumstances come.

Paul contrasts Adam's disobedience with Christ's obedience that brings righteousness, supporting the prayer's claim that justifying righteousness is completed in Christ rather than produced by the believer.
Paul celebrates death being swallowed up in victory through Jesus Christ, which directly supports the prayer's confidence that Christ has defeated death.
The risen Jesus declares that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him, grounding the prayer's trust in his universal power.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original request for 'way-tokens' like Gideon could be misunderstood as encouraging believers to demand signs from God. The adaptation frames it as asking for patient encouragement and courage for obedience, rather than treating Gideon's fleece as a normal method of guidance.

The line asking that life not extend beyond usefulness reflects a strong Puritan concern for fruitful service and mortality. It could sound harsh or imply that human worth depends on productivity, so the adaptation preserves the desire for God-given usefulness while avoiding the idea that a person's value ends when visible usefulness declines.

The prayer addresses Jesus directly with covenantal and providential language. This is within historic Christian prayer, though some readers may more commonly address such language to the Father through the Son.
significant_interpretive_choices: 'Blessings with bitter things' was rendered as God using hard circumstances to awaken and strengthen faith, not as a claim that suffering is pleasant or good in itself.

'Cast me not under the feet of pride, injustice, riches, worldly greatness, selfish oppression of men' was interpreted as a plea for protection both from oppressive external powers and from the corrupting values behind them.
'Finished justifying righteousness' was interpreted as Christ's completed obedience and saving work as the ground of justification.

'Marked with thine own blood in the court of forgiving mercy' was rendered as covenant confidence secured by Christ's blood before God's forgiving mercy, preserving the legal/covenantal image without reproducing archaic phrasing.
